new_statements.quote: provide sufficient evidence, despite the challenges mentioned above, to propose a bounded, quantity-sensitive, variable accent system for Domung. Specifically, accent falls within a bisyllabic window on the left edge of words with the first syllable as the preferred accent location as shown by (60). [...] If the first (target) syllable within the accent window is lighter than the second syllable, then accent shifts to the second syllable as shown by (61) in accordance with the syllable weight scale detailed below in (62). [...] Lastly, the final syllable of a word may not be accented; therefore, in bisyllabic words, accent is placed on the first syllable even if the first syllable is lighter than the second syllable as shown by (63).

new_statements.rule_in_words: No tone. Primary accent falls on the first or second syllable (left-edge two-syllable window): on the first syllable by default, shifting to the second if the first is lighter on the scale closed/long (C)VC, (C)VV(C) > CV > V > (C)ə; the final syllable is never accented, so disyllables are always initial (e.g. ˈɢaɴ.ɢa.boq 'vine sp.', ˈbo.ram 'grub' vs a.ˈsa.da 'left', də.ˈmu.na 'pitpit sp.'). Duration is the main correlate; intensity is not; final syllables carry a pitch drop.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described for Domung (the term appears only in the survey of other Finisterre languages, e.g. Awara).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 74: 'while this analysis accounts for the vast majority of the words within the corpus, exceptions do exist and more in-depth research of the accent system is needed in order to understand these exceptions.' One of nine consulted speakers judged that Domung has no accent at all (p. 71). The weight scale, especially the claim that presence of an onset adds weight, is called tentative (p. 73).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in isolated elicited words (1600+-word Dekereke corpus, citation forms) of the central Buwa Me dialect; native-speaker intuition on 14 words (88% agreement) plus preliminary acoustic cues. The relationship to phrase-level stress is explicitly left for future research (p. 74). Nothing describes the Gabutamon (Sikikon Me) variety itself.
new_statements.identity_note: gabu1248 'Gabutamon' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 change request 2009-044 (adopted 2010-01-18;, secs. 4-5) merged Gabutamon [gav] into Domung [dev] = Glottolog domu1246 (Yupna, Finisterre-Huon; Madang Province, PNG). Gabutamon is a village at the western end of the Domung dialect chain and, per Moe 2023 p. 6, the primary village of the Síkíkon Me dialect. The quoted statement describes the central Buwa Me dialect of Domung (Moe 2023 p. 7), not the Gabutamon/Síkíkon variety, for which no description exists. The catalog entry belongs under domu1246 (a domu1246 folder with the same thesis already exists; gabu1248 should be recorded as a retired duplicate of domu1246, not as a separate language.

sources.note: Ch. 7 'Tone and Accent' (pp. 67-79): no tone; a bounded, quantity-sensitive, variable accent system: accent falls in a bisyllabic window at the left edge, first syllable preferred, shifting to the second syllable if the first is lighter on a weight scale (CVC/CVV > CV > V > Cə); final syllable never accented, so disyllables are always initial (pp. 72-74). Acoustic cues: duration correlates, intensity does not, final syllables show pitch drop (p. 79). Exceptions exist; word- vs phrase-level stress left for future work (p. 74). sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2009. Change Request 2009-044 (submitted by Sara Van Cott, SIL-PNG, 7 Jul 2009; adopted 2010-01-18): merge Gabutamon [gav] into Domung [dev]; create Yout Wam [ytw]. 7 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Sec. 4 (pp. 2-3): Gabutamon village is one end of the Domung dialect chain (Gabutamon; Maum/Kosit; Wakopop/Bobongat; Aunon; Ayengket; Sibgou/Kian/Dirit/Swantan/Maramung), >=70% lexical similarity with central Domung villages; speakers self-identify as Domung. Cites Gray 2007 ms.

Phonology survey p. 66: 'Stress is phonemic in Rawa but probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat. In none of these languages does it carry a heavy functional load.' -- 'Yupna' here is the Kewieng/Nokopo language, not Domung; nothing on Domung/Gabutamon stress.
